claim: Passive immunization with plasma from recovered patients has a long and generally successful history.
source: Passive immunization with plasma from patients who have seroconverted to and recovered from infection with a pathogen has a long and generally successful history.
evidence: Supported by citations to historical use cases

claim: Passive immunization has been used extensively against influenza virus.
source: It has been used extensively against influenza virus and on a small scale during the 1995 and 2014–2015 Ebola epidemics (Brown et al., 2018; Mupapa et al., 1999; Mair-Jenkins et al., 2015; Hung et al., 2011; Luke et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations

claim: Passive immunization was used on a small scale during the 1995 and 2014-2015 Ebola epidemics.
source: It has been used extensively against influenza virus and on a small scale during the 1995 and 2014–2015 Ebola epidemics (Brown et al., 2018; Mupapa et al., 1999; Mair-Jenkins et al., 2015; Hung et al., 2011; Luke et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations

claim: Purified polyclonal immunoglobulin from convalescents has been administered prophylactically after exposure to infectious virus.
source: Purified polyclonal (sometimes referred to as polyvalent) immunoglobulin (Ig) from convalescents has been administered prophylactically after exposure to infectious virus (Young, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Young, 2019

claim: Highly specific and broadly active neutralizing monoclonal antibodies have been developed against several viruses in recent years.
source: In recent years, highly specific and often broadly active neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (MAbs) have been developed against several viruses, as a more advanced substitute for patient plasma (Caskey et al., 2019; Corti et al., 2016; Corti et al., 2017; Walker and Burton, 2018; Wec et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations

claim: Passive immunization methods are being considered for treating COVID-19.
source: These methods are now being considered for treating COVID-19, the disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus (Dhama et al., 2020; Jawhara, 2020; Ju et al., 2020; Zhou and Zhao, 2020; Accorsi et al., 2020; Bloch et al., 2020; Sullivan and Roback, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations

claim: Convalescent plasma infusion showed apparent benefits with no adverse side effects in SARS-CoV-1 patients.
source: Several reports describe apparent benefits, with no adverse side effects, when convalescent plasma was infused into patients with SARS-CoV-1 or SARS-CoV-2 infection (Table 1; Cheng et al., 2005; Yeh et al., 2005; Soo et al., 2004; Shen et al., 2020; Duan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Ahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Table 1

claim: Convalescent plasma infusion showed apparent benefits with no adverse side effects in SARS-CoV-2 patients.
source: Several reports describe apparent benefits, with no adverse side effects, when convalescent plasma was infused into patients with SARS-CoV-1 or SARS-CoV-2 infection (Table 1; Cheng et al., 2005; Yeh et al., 2005; Soo et al., 2004; Shen et al., 2020; Duan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Ahn et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Table 1

claim: The US FDA has approved plasma immunotherapy for COVID-19.
source: The US Food and Drug Administration has recently approved plasma immunotherapy for this purpose, and has outlined safety criteria (https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/investigational-new-drug-ind-or-device-exemption-ide-process-cber/recommendations-investigational-covid-19-convalescent-plasma).
evidence: Direct statement about FDA approval with reference to FDA website

claim: The FDA has called for randomized clinical trials to determine the efficacy of convalescent plasma to treat COVID-19.
source: To determine the efficacy of convalescent plasma to treat COVID-19, the FDA has called for randomized clinical trials and encouraged investigational new drug applications (Bloch et al., 2020; Sullivan and Roback, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bloch et al., 2020 and Sullivan and Roback, 2020

claim: A major goal of viral vaccine development is the induction of strong and broadly active neutralizing antibodies.
source: A major goal of viral vaccine development is the induction of strong and broadly active neutralizing antibodies (NAbs), and that goal applies also to SARS-CoV-2 (Dhama et al., 2020; Graham, 2020; Amanat and Krammer, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations and established vaccine development principles

claim: The entry of SARS-CoV-2 into cells is initiated by the interaction of the receptor-binding domain of the viral Spike glycoprotein with ACE2.
source: The entry of SARS-CoV-2 into cells is initiated by the interaction of the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the viral Spike (S) glycoprotein with the angiotensin converting enzyme-2 (ACE2), which acts as a receptor for the virus on the target cell surface (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Ou et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2020 and Ou et al., 2020

claim: ACE2 acts as a receptor for SARS-CoV-2 on the target cell surface.
source: The entry of SARS-CoV-2 into cells is initiated by the interaction of the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the viral Spike (S) glycoprotein with the angiotensin converting enzyme-2 (ACE2), which acts as a receptor for the virus on the target cell surface (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Ou et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2020 and Ou et al., 2020

claim: The most potent neutralizing antibodies are directed to the RBD.
source: The most potent NAbs are directed to the RBD and some may act by simply competing with the receptor for binding to the S-protein.
evidence: Based on inference from the mechanism of viral entry and antibody function

claim: Some neutralizing antibodies may act by competing with the receptor for binding to the S-protein.
source: The most potent NAbs are directed to the RBD and some may act by simply competing with the receptor for binding to the S-protein.
evidence: Based on inference from mechanism of action

claim: Antibodies to SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV generally do not cross-neutralize SARS-CoV-2.
source: Antibodies to SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV generally do not cross-neutralize SARS-CoV-2; although cross-reactive antibodies are frequently detected in S-protein ELISA (Ju et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Ou et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2005; Quinlan et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations

claim: Cross-reactive antibodies to SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV are frequently detected in S-protein ELISA.
source: Antibodies to SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV generally do not cross-neutralize SARS-CoV-2; although cross-reactive antibodies are frequently detected in S-protein ELISA (Ju et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Ou et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2005; Quinlan et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations

claim: The S-protein-specific NAb S309 was isolated from memory B cells of a patient who had recovered from CoV-1 infection in 2003.
source: Recently, however, the S-protein-specific NAb S309, isolated from memory B cells of a patient who had recovered from CoV-1 infection in 2003, was shown to neutralize both SARS-CoV-1 and −2 potently by ligating the RBD.
evidence: Based on inference from the cited study

claim: S309 neutralizes both SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 potently by ligating the RBD.
source: Recently, however, the S-protein-specific NAb S309, isolated from memory B cells of a patient who had recovered from CoV-1 infection in 2003, was shown to neutralize both SARS-CoV-1 and −2 potently by ligating the RBD.
evidence: Based on inference from the cited study

claim: The S309 epitope comprises glycans and is conserved.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy and binding assays demonstrated that the conserved S309 epitope comprises glycans and that in spite of the specificity of the Mab for the RBD, it does not interfere with ACE2 binding (Pinto et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pinto et al., 2020 describing cryo-EM and binding assays

claim: S309 does not interfere with ACE2 binding despite its specificity for the RBD.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy and binding assays demonstrated that the conserved S309 epitope comprises glycans and that in spite of the specificity of the Mab for the RBD, it does not interfere with ACE2 binding (Pinto et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pinto et al., 2020 describing cryo-EM and binding assays

claim: The neutralizing potency of antibodies against the RBD may be determined by their affinity for the S-protein and the affinity of the S-protein for ACE2 when they act by a competitive mechanism.
source: The neutralizing potency of antibodies against the RBD may be determined not only by their own affinity for the S-protein but also by the affinity of the latter for ACE2, at least when they act by a competitive mechanism (Ju et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ju et al., 2020

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 S-protein has a 4-20-fold higher affinity for ACE2 than its counterpart from SARS-CoV-1.
source: In this context, it is notable that the SARS-CoV-2 S-protein has a 4–20-fold higher affinity for ACE2 than its counterpart from SARS-CoV-1 (35, 37).
evidence: Supported by citations (35, 37)

claim: Most neutralizing antibodies to SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 are directed to the RBD.
source: Although most NAbs to SARS-CoV-1 and −2 are directed to the RBD (Pinto et al., 2020; Coughlin et al., 2007; Greenough et al., 2005; Sui et al., 2004; ter Meulen et al., 2006; van den Brink et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2007), some antibodies that recognize the SARS-CoV-1 S2 fragment can also neutralize (Duan et al., 2005; Elshabrawy et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations

claim: Some antibodies that recognize the SARS-CoV-1 S2 fragment can neutralize the virus.
source: Although most NAbs to SARS-CoV-1 and −2 are directed to the RBD (Pinto et al., 2020; Coughlin et al., 2007; Greenough et al., 2005; Sui et al., 2004; ter Meulen et al., 2006; van den Brink et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2007), some antibodies that recognize the SARS-CoV-1 S2 fragment can also neutralize (Duan et al., 2005; Elshabrawy et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duan et al., 2005 and Elshabrawy et al., 2012

claim: Antibodies to the ectodomain of SARS-CoV-1 protein Orf3a have neutralizing activity.
source: In addition, antibodies to the ectodomain of another surface-exposed SARS-CoV-1 protein, Orf3a, are also reported to have neutralizing activity, while antibodies to the M and E proteins can potentiate neutralization (Akerström et al., 2006; Buchholz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Akerström et al., 2006 and Buchholz et al., 2004

claim: Antibodies to the M and E proteins of SARS-CoV-1 can potentiate neutralization.
source: In addition, antibodies to the ectodomain of another surface-exposed SARS-CoV-1 protein, Orf3a, are also reported to have neutralizing activity, while antibodies to the M and E proteins can potentiate neutralization (Akerström et al., 2006; Buchholz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Akerström et al., 2006 and Buchholz et al., 2004

claim: Passive and active immunization approaches to COVID-19 are generally focused on neutralizing antibodies against the S1-protein.
source: Nonetheless, passive and active immunization approaches to COVID-19 are generally focused on NAbs against the S1-protein.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of current immunization strategies

claim: The NAb response in SARS-CoV-1 patients who later succumbed to infection was faster than in those who recovered.
source: Surprisingly, the NAb response in patients who later succumbed to the infection has been found to be faster than in those who recovered; in the patients who later died, the titers had peaked around day 15 after the onset of symptoms, whereas similar titers and extents of neutralization were reached only after day 20 in the patients who recovered (Zhang et al., 2006; Ho et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2006 and Ho et al., 2005

claim: In SARS-CoV-1 patients who later died, NAb titers peaked around day 15 after the onset of symptoms.
source: Surprisingly, the NAb response in patients who later succumbed to the infection has been found to be faster than in those who recovered; in the patients who later died, the titers had peaked around day 15 after the onset of symptoms, whereas similar titers and extents of neutralization were reached only after day 20 in the patients who recovered (Zhang et al., 2006; Ho et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2006 and Ho et al., 2005

claim: In SARS-CoV-1 patients who recovered, NAb titers reached similar levels only after day 20.

claim: NAb titers in moribund SARS-CoV-1 patients declined or disappeared after the early rise as their conditions deteriorated towards death.

source: As NAb titers rise, however, viral loads decline, presumably because virus replication diminishes (Wölfel et al., 2020; To et al., 2020).

claim: In plasma from 175 patients who recovered from mild COVID-19, NAb and S-binding-antibody titers correlated positively with age and CRP levels.
source: In plasma collected from 175 patients who had recovered from mild COVID-19, NAb and S-binding-antibody titers correlated positively with age and CRP (C-reactive protein) levels, but negatively with lymphocyte counts; and the NAbs did not cross-neutralize SARS-CoV-1 (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2020

claim: In plasma from 175 patients who recovered from mild COVID-19, NAb and S-binding-antibody titers correlated negatively with lymphocyte counts.
source: In plasma collected from 175 patients who had recovered from mild COVID-19, NAb and S-binding-antibody titers correlated positively with age and CRP (C-reactive protein) levels, but negatively with lymphocyte counts; and the NAbs did not cross-neutralize SARS-CoV-1 (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2020

claim: NAbs from patients who recovered from mild COVID-19 did not cross-neutralize SARS-CoV-1.
source: In plasma collected from 175 patients who had recovered from mild COVID-19, NAb and S-binding-antibody titers correlated positively with age and CRP (C-reactive protein) levels, but negatively with lymphocyte counts; and the NAbs did not cross-neutralize SARS-CoV-1 (Wu et al., 2020).

claim: The positive correlation between NAb responses and age contrasts with a general decline in the vigor of new B-cell responses in the elderly.
source: The positive correlation between NAb responses and age contrasts with a general decline in the vigor of new B-cell responses in the elderly (Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009), but raises the question whether the pre-response viral load was correlated with age, which in turn correlates with disease severity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009 and inference about the contrast

claim: Higher binding-antibody titers to the nucleocapsid protein N were found in patients who recovered from SARS-CoV-1 than in those who did not.
source: Other studies have shown higher binding-antibody titers to the nucleocapsid protein N in patients who recovered than in those who did not (Wu et al., 2020; Leung et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2020 and Leung et al., 2004

claim: Antibodies to the N-protein completely lack neutralizing capacity.

claim: Production of antibodies to the N-protein might reflect the strength of T-helper cell responses.
source: Such antibodies to the N-protein, which is internal and thus not exposed on the surface of the virion, completely lack neutralizing capacity but their production might reflect the strength of T-helper cell responses (Klasse et al., 2012).

claim: Anti-S antibodies protect against lethal CoV challenge and clear the virus in mice and ferrets.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection protected macaques against a second challenge, which was attributed to the development of protective antibodies.

claim: Benefits such as lower viral loads and earlier release from hospital were noted in retrospective analyses of SARS-CoV-1 patients given plasma with high NAb titers.

claim: The RBD-binding antibody endpoint titers in the transfused plasma were >1000 and the neutralization endpoint titers were >40.

claim: After plasma transfusion, body temperatures normalized in the five COVID-19 patients.

claim: After plasma transfusion, organ-failure and respiratory-function scores improved to various extents in the five COVID-19 patients.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 ELISA and NAb titers increased after plasma transfusion, reflecting the antibody-content of the transfused plasma.
